origin.fact: A fairly recent man-made colour form of the common aquarium angelfish. This wholesaler first got it from Sri Lanka in 2006, and almost all big ornamental fish farms now produce it.
This wholesaler thinks several species were probably involved in making the domestic angelfish, so it does not see much point in giving a species name.
It came out of gold angelfish lines.
It came from gold angelfish lines.
Hobby lore says platinums from Asian farms were used to bring out the blue gene. The source names no breeder and gives no date.
Crossing a gold with a Philippine Blue and then breeding the young together produces platinums, along with wild-type, gold and blue fish.

looks.fact: Solid silvery white with no bars. Young fish have a white sheen, and adults can take on a green or blue tint.
The white sheen of young fish turns greenish-blue as they mature.
Silvery white body with black eyes. The black eyes separate it from the red-eyed albino.
This wholesaler describes its stock as snow-white with red eyes that are somewhat sensitive to light. This is the opposite of the black-eyed description used elsewhere.
Show fish must be ghostly white with no trace of bars. Any leftover stripes or yellowing disqualifies a fish, so platinums need stricter culling than other lines.
Looks best under bright light in a planted tank.

lines.fact: Platinum Pearlscale, sometimes sold as 'White Pearl', is the platinum combined with the pearlscale gene.

keeping.fact: Care, temperature and food are the same as for the ordinary aquarium angelfish.
Needs at least about 114 litres (30 US gallons). Prefers soft, slightly acidic water with KH 1–5.
Rated semi-aggressive. Does best in a well-planted tank with plenty of swimming room.
Omnivore. Feed good flakes plus live or frozen brine shrimp and bloodworms, and add some plant matter.

breeding.fact: Breeds like other angelfish. Let a pair form, then give them an angled flat surface to spawn on.

Platinum is recessive. This source gives the genotype as g/g pb/pb. A platinum crossed with a wild-type fish gives only normal-looking carriers. Breeding those carriers together gives golds, platinums, blues and wild-type fish.
Caused by two copies of a recessive gene, so platinum × platinum should breed true.
This source gives a different explanation: two copies of gold on a stripeless background, at minimum ggSS. Normal-looking fish may hide these genes, and only test crosses reveal them.
This wholesaler links the colour loss to a gene for complete albinism.
Angelfish spawn readily at 27–29 °C in slightly soft water.

health.fact: In red-eyed stock, the eyes are somewhat sensitive to light.
Heavy inbreeding (a coefficient above 0.25 over three generations) is linked to smaller spawns, spinal deformities and weaker immunity. That matters for lines kept closed to fix a recessive colour.

buying.fact: Pick fish that are pure white with no faint bars or yellow cast.
Check the eye colour. A true platinum has black eyes, and red eyes mean an albino.
For breeding, add unrelated fish from a trusted breeder now and then, and keep pedigree records.
